hints: Look very closely at Fig. 6.1 at the shapes on the cell surfaces and the shape of the EGF triangles - what fits together on cell A and what does not fit on cell B?
Think about the general rule for signalling molecules - why does a hormone or growth factor only affect target cells with the right receptor protein?
walkthrough:
Spot the Binding Difference in Fig. 6.1**
You can see the small triangles labelled EGF sitting exactly on the Y-shaped receptors on top of cell A. On cell B the surface receptors are a different rounded U-shape and the EGF triangles stay free above the cell. So binding has happened on A but not on B.

Explain With Receptor Specificity**
A cell only responds if it has the correct receptor protein. The binding site must be complementary in shape and charge to the signalling molecule. Cell A has EGF receptors, so EGF can bind and trigger the move from $G_1$ to S phase. Cell B lacks EGF receptors, so no binding, no signal, and it remains in interphase.
Final answer: EGF binds to receptors on cell A but not on cell B; the receptors on cell A are complementary / specific in shape to EGF, whereas those on cell B are not.

hints: Think about what the cell must make in $G_1$ before it can copy its DNA and divide, and why making mRNA for that would be difficult when chromosomes are tightly condensed in mitosis.
walkthrough:
Link mRNA to Protein Need in $G_1$**
Remember mRNA is made by transcription and then used to make protein. In $G_1$ the cell is growing, making new organelles, enzymes and proteins needed for DNA replication in the S phase. So lots of transcription is needed. In mitosis the job is just to separate chromosomes already made, not to make new protein, and the DNA is tightly coiled and condensed so RNA polymerase cannot access genes to transcribe them.
Final answer: More proteins are made in $G_1$ for growth / for DNA synthesis in S phase, requiring mRNA by transcription; during mitosis DNA is highly condensed so transcription cannot occur.

hints: Start with what a new DNA strand is built from - what small building blocks must be available in the nucleus during S phase?
Think about what provides energy for this endergonic polymerisation and what unwinds the helix.
Now think about which enzymes join the new nucleotides together into a continuous strand and join Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
walkthrough:
Building Blocks and Energy**
To synthesise DNA you need a supply of activated free DNA nucleotides containing the bases A, T, C and G. Their addition is powered by ATP which provides energy for DNA synthesis.

Enzymes That Build and Join**
DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides together in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction to form the new polynucleotide strand. DNA ligase seals nicks and joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand. Helicase (with topoisomerase / gyrase to relieve tension) unwinds the double helix to expose the template strands.
Final answer: Any three from: ATP; activated / free DNA nucleotides; DNA polymerase; DNA ligase; helicase / topoisomerase / gyrase.

hints: Look at Fig. 6.2 - region X is the narrow pinched point in the middle where the two sister chromatids of this metaphase chromosome meet.
Think about what must hold the two chromatids together until anaphase and what must attach to spindle microtubules to move them.
walkthrough:
Name Region X**
In metaphase the chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at a constricted region. That region labelled X is the centromere, with the kinetochore protein complex on its surface.

Link Structure to Function in Mitosis**
Its structure lets it do two jobs. It holds the sister chromatids together until anaphase, ensuring they line up on the metaphase plate. It is also where spindle fibres attach, so when the centromere splits the chromatids can be pulled to opposite poles.
Final answer: name: centromere (accept kinetochore); function: holds / joins sister chromatids together; site of attachment to spindle microtubules.

hints: Remember what anaphase does to the chromosome in Fig. 6.2 - the centromere splits, so how many separate units should you draw and where should they be going?
Think about the shape of each separated chromatid - Fig. 6.2 shows one arm longer than the other, and the centromere leads the way to the pole when pulled by the spindle.
walkthrough:
From One Chromosome to Two Chromatids**
In metaphase in Fig. 6.2 you see one chromosome made of two sister chromatids joined at X. In anaphase the centromere divides, so you must draw them as two completely separate identical units, one moving toward the left pole and one toward the right pole. Do not draw a joined X-shape again.

Keep the Shape and Orientation Correct**
Each chromatid keeps the same morphology as in Fig. 6.2, with one arm clearly longer / larger than the other. Because spindle fibres pull on the centromere, draw each as a V-shape with the point (centromere) leading and pointing toward its pole and the arms trailing behind toward the equator.
Final answer: Draw two separate identical chromatids, one near each pole; each with one arm larger / longer than the other; each V-shaped with centromere pointing toward the nearest pole.
